extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, students, and general users of English seeking guidance on grammar and usage
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and usage guidance for English pronouns (personal, possessive, reflexive, demonstrative, reciprocal, interrogative, relative, indefinite) and adjectives (types, articles, position, degrees). Covers case, agreement, capitalization, punctuation, and common errors with examples and rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns are classified by type (personal, possessive, reflexive/intensive, demonstrative, reciprocal, interrogative, relative, indefinite) and may function as more than one type depending on use (e.g., that as demonstrative, relative, or adjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize each pronoun’s role in context; many pronouns (except personal) can serve multiple functions. Examples illustrate different categories and cross-uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and function of personal pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal pronoun shows person (first/second/third), number, gender, and case by its form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person for speaker (I/we), second for addressee (you), third for others (he/she/it/they). The pronoun’s form should reflect person, number, gender, and grammatical case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of personal pronoun I
rubrics_metrics.description: The first-person-singular pronoun I is always capitalized no matter where it appears in the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other pronouns are capitalized only at the beginning of a sentence or as part of an honorific title (e.g., Her Majesty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-person 'you' takes plural verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Although you can be singular or plural in meaning, it always takes a plural verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when addressing one person, use plural verb agreement with you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominative vs objective case: four essential rules
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Subject of a clause → nominative; (2) object of a verb → objective; (3) object of a preposition → objective; (4) subject of an infinitive → objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four tests to determine pronoun case. Examples: he is vice president (nominative); she thanked him (objective); keep this between you and me (objective); Jim wanted her to sing (her as subject of infinitive → objective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun agreement with antecedent (gender and number)
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal pronoun agrees with its antecedent noun in both gender and number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pronouns match antecedent (e.g., John ... he; Sheila ... she). Use appropriate gender forms for third-person singular; consider personification conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender and personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person-singular pronouns directly express gender; pronouns can enhance personification when feminine or masculine pronouns are used for nonliving things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of traditional uses (ships called 'she') and modern sensibilities; choose gendered pronouns intentionally in personification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special personal-pronoun case rules
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Pronoun as clause subject or following conjunction but preceding verb → nominative; (2) object of verb/preposition → objective; (3) multiple objects in a prepositional phrase → all objective; (4) subject of an infinitive → objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these specific situational rules (examples provided) to choose nominative vs objective forms correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun after linking verb should be nominative
rubrics_metrics.description: A pronoun serving as the complement of a be-verb or other linking verb should be in the nominative case (predicate nominative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined/formal usage: This is he (not This is him). Expect informal usage to differ; formal contexts prefer nominative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns after 'than' or 'as — case depends on meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The case of a pronoun following comparative constructions depends on what is being compared; elliptical constructions can be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ambiguous, reword to avoid elliptical constructions and ensure intended case (examples show nominate vs objective interpretations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generic masculine 'he' without care
rubrics_metrics.description: He, him, his have traditionally been used generically for an indeterminate gender, but this use is declining and may be regarded as sexist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gender-neutral constructions; respect individuals’ stated pronoun preferences; consult related sections (5.251-60) for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of 'it' (non-gender, expletive, anticipatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: It can eliminate gender, refer to clauses/phrases/thoughts, act as grammatical subject for time/weather/distance, serve as an expletive anticipating the true subject/object, or stand in for an indefinite referent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple functions of it (e.g., it is possible that...). Use appropriately depending on syntactic role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite uses of we/you/they (including editorial we)
rubrics_metrics.description: We, you, and they can be used indefinitely without explicit antecedents to refer to persons in general; 'editorial we' is when an individual speaks for a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these indefinite forms intentionally (e.g., 'from these results we can draw...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular 'they' usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular they/them/their (and variant themself) is commonly used in speech/informal writing for a person of unspecified or nonbinary gender; like singular you, singular they takes a plural verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago historically recommended avoiding singular they in formal writing, though acceptance is increasing; respect a person's stated pronoun preference; note editorial endorsements and regional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and uses of possessive pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessive pronouns (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) qualify nouns as limiting adjectives; independent possessives (mine, ours, yours, his, hers, its, theirs) can stand alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent possessives can function as nouns (subject/object). Use double possessive constructions with 'of' + -'s when appropriate (that letter of Sheila’s = that letter of hers).

rubrics_metrics.name: No apostrophes in possessive pronouns; watch homophones
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the possessive personal pronouns is spelled with an apostrophe; common errors occur by confusing them with contractions (it's vs its; your vs you're; whose vs who’s; their/there/they’re).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert apostrophes into possessive pronouns. Be alert for homophone errors and teach common confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive vs intensive pronouns: correct functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflexive pronouns (myself, ourselves, yourself, etc.) serve as objects referring back to the subject; intensive pronouns repeat the antecedent for emphasis and are in apposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish functions to avoid errors: don't use reflexive forms as subjects or as objects that do not refer to the subject (POOR vs BETTER examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common misuse of -self forms (avoid 'myself' as subject/object misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using myself in compound subjects or as an object when it doesn't refer back to the subject (e.g., 'The staff and myself thank you' is incorrect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace with I (subject) or me (object) as appropriate; examples show POOR/BETTER alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative pronouns: clarity of antecedent and human reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstratives (this/that/these/those) point to antecedents in text and must have a clear antecedent; a demonstrative standing alone cannot refer to a human antecedent—it must be followed by a noun denoting a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstratives to indicate proximity in space/time/thought. Ensure antecedent clarity to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal pronouns: each other vs one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal pronouns (each other, one another) express mutual relationships; each other traditionally for two, one another for more than two; can take genitive -'s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the reciprocal that matches intended number; compare meaning vs plural reflexive uses (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogative pronouns: who/what/which and cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatives ask questions. The three interrogatives are who, what, and which; who declines (who/whom/whose). Who as subject or predicate nominative; whom as object of verb or preposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whom for objects (e.g., 'Whom did you see?'); use who for subjects. Teach declining forms and prepositional usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions among who/which/what as referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is universal/general for persons; which and what are selective or limited when followed by a noun naming a person; which refers to animals/things, what refers to nonliving things or broad sets; when applied to a person, what often asks about character/occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick interrogative that matches scope of expected answer (general vs limited vs character/quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative pronouns: who/which/what/that definitions and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative pronouns introduce dependent clauses and relate them to independent clauses. Who refers to humans (declines), which to animals/things, what to nonliving things, and that to human/animal/thing in any person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that for restrictive clauses, which for nonrestrictive clauses, and who for people; consider relative adjective functions when qualifying noun elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement and case interactions with relative pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative pronoun agrees with its antecedent in gender, person, and number. A personal pronoun following a relative pronoun and referring to the same antecedent takes that antecedent’s gender/number. A personal pronoun does not govern the case of a relative pronoun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure relative pronoun matches antecedent; when constructions sound archaic or awkward, rephrase to clearer alternatives (preventive grammar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positional nuances of relative pronouns and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative pronoun is nominative when no subject intervenes between it and the verb. If intervening words occur, the relative is governed by the following verb or a verb/preposition within the intervening clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze clause internals to determine case and avoid misassignment when words intervene (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent placement for clarity with relative pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: For clarity, a relative pronoun’s antecedent should immediately precede the pronoun; antecedents may also be phrases or clauses but can create ambiguity when distant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When separation creates ambiguity, reword; examples show POOR/BETTER rewrites to eliminate unclear antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of restrictive vs nonrestrictive relative pronouns (that vs which)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use that for restrictive (essential) relative clauses and which for nonrestrictive (parenthetical) clauses; what can be used when there is no expressed antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select relative pronoun based on clause necessity to sentence meaning. See cross-references for punctuation rules (nonrestrictive with commas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative pronoun agreement when antecedent includes 'one of those'
rubrics_metrics.description: When one is part of a noun phrase with a plural noun (one of the few/one of those), the relative pronoun that follows takes the plural noun as its antecedent—treat the pronoun as plural and use a plural verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Lily is one of those people who are famous for being famous' (use are).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genitive forms for relative pronouns and 'whose' vs 'of which'
rubrics_metrics.description: Genitive forms such as 'of whom' and 'of which' are correct but can sound old-fashioned; whose substitutes for 'of which' and is widely accepted and smoother even with nonhuman antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may rephrase to avoid awkward forms; using whose for nonhuman antecedents is acceptable and often preferable for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound relative pronouns with -ever
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever, whomever, whichever, and whatever form compound relatives adding -ever and apply universally to any or all persons or things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand their broad applicability; use case determined by the pronoun’s function within its clause (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining who vs whom in complex clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Case for who/whom can be hard to see in inverted or nested clauses; determine the pronoun’s function in its own clause (not the main sentence) to choose the correct case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast interrogatives into standard subject-verb-object order to test case. Examples show common errors and corrected forms (e.g., 'Whom should I say is calling?' → 'Who should I say is calling?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite pronouns: number and distributive usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefinite pronouns (another, any, both, each, either, neither, none, one, other, some, such, and compounds) generally represent unspecified objects; each/either/neither are distributive. They have number—usually singular as subjects—but can sometimes carry a plural sense in informal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat indefinite pronouns as singular for verb agreement in formal writing; be aware of informal plural uses (e.g., 'nobody ... they'). Possessives may take -'s or else's for forms like 'anybody else's.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and formation of adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjective modifies a noun or pronoun (describing word) and can describe sort, number, size, possession, etc. Many adjectives derive from nouns/verbs/adjectives and are formed with suffixes (-able, -al, -ful, -less, etc.), though many have no distinctive ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize function-based identification of adjectives. Use suffix patterns as helpful cues but rely on syntactic role to determine adjective status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper adjectives capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper adjective derived from a proper name begins with a capital letter (e.g., New York minute, Cuban cigar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper names used attributively remain capitalized but do not cause the modified noun to be capitalized; avoid awkward place-name adjectives that require commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles as limiting adjectives and their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles (the, a, an) are limiting adjectives: the signals definite/specific reference; a/an signal indefinite/nonspecific. Some idiomatic or contextual uses invert specificity (indefinite used specifically or definite generically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the/A based on definiteness. Use a vs an according to sound, not spelling; examples include abbreviations and initialisms (a BTU vs an MBA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing 'a' or 'an' by sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection between 'a' and 'an' depends on the initial sound of the following word: consonant sound → a; vowel sound → an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to abbreviations/acronyms based on their pronounced initial sound (e.g., a PDF, an ATM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles with coordinate nouns and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: With coordinate nouns, an article may appear before each noun but is not necessary; repeat the article when distinguishing concepts or adding emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nouns form a single idea, don't repeat the article; if distinguishing, repeat (e.g., 'the time, the money, and the effort').

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of article choice on meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing articles can alter meaning (e.g., 'an officer and gentleman' vs 'an officer and a friend' implies different numbers of escorts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise with articles to avoid unintended ambiguity; use hyphenation or repetition when needed for clarity (e.g., red-and-blue cloth vs the red cloth and the blue cloth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted (zero) article usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of an article (zero article) can change meaning and is common in idiomatic references to time, illness, transport, routines, meals, etc. (e.g., 'go to bed' vs 'make the bed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize standard idiomatic zero-article constructions and their semantic effects (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles as pronoun substitutes in forms
rubrics_metrics.description: An article may substitute for a pronoun in blanks or forms where a possessive might be expected (e.g., 'the blanks in a patient who develops the described rash on __ hands should inform __ doctor' may take the).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use article substitution where appropriate to fit noun phrase constructions in forms or templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of adjectives: attributive vs postpositive vs predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes: adjectives usually precede nouns (attributive). Adjectives may follow nouns (postpositive) for emphasis, idiom, predicate usage, or appositive modification. Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs and modify the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard adjective positions; employ postpositive only in idiomatic or emphatic cases; identify predicate adjectives as those following linking verbs (examples and exceptions explained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjective after possessive and adjective modifying pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: When a noun phrase includes a possessive, adjectives follow the possessive (children's athletic shoes). When modifying a pronoun, adjectives usually follow the pronoun or function as a predicate adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of adjective placement relative to possessives and pronouns for intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date expressions as adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Month-year or month-day date used as an adjective needs no hyphen or comma (October 31 festivities); full month-day-year dates traditionally take commas (May 27, 2016, ceremonies) but are awkward and best avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructions that avoid awkward commas in adjectival date phrases (e.g., 'commencement ceremonies on May 27, 2016' or better, avoid full date as adjectival phrase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of adjectives: positive, comparative, superlative
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives are gradable into positive (hard), comparative (harder), and superlative (hardest). Comparatives express relationships between two things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative to compare typically two items; form comparatives/superlatives per morphological/analytical rules (examples implied).
